- $v_{\text{ret}} = \dfrac{30 \times 40}{\sqrt{900 + 1600}} = \dfrac{1200}{50} = 24$ m/s.
- Falling from rest to $0.6v_T$: $t = \dfrac{v_T}{g}\tanh^{-1}0.6 = 4.082 \times \tfrac12\ln 4 \approx 2.83$ s.

The fall (2.83 s) takes *longer* than the rise (2.63 s). On the way up, drag adds to gravity;
on the way down, it subtracts. The whole flight takes about 5.46 s instead of 6.12 s.

## Linear and quadratic drag side by side

Give both models the package from Lesson 13, with the same terminal velocity, 24.5 m/s. Both
then have the same time scale, $v_T/g = 2.5$ s, yet the quadratic one gets close to $v_T$
sooner: at $t = 5$ s it is at 23.6 m/s against 21.2 m/s. The reason is that at any speed
below $v_T$, $kv^2 = mg(v/v_T)^2$ is smaller than $\gamma v = mg(v/v_T)$, so quadratic drag
holds the object back less until it is nearly at terminal speed.

```plot
{"x": [0, 12], "y": [0, 30], "xLabel": "t (s)", "yLabel": "v (m/s)", "functions": [{"f": "24.5tanh(0.4x)"}, {"f": "24.5(1 - exp(-0.4x))"}, {"f": "24.5", "dashed": true}, {"f": "9.8x", "dashed": true, "to": 2.5, "label": "no drag"}], "caption": "Same terminal velocity, 24.5 m/s (dashed line): the quadratic-drag curve (upper) approaches it faster than the linear-drag curve (lower)."}
```

## Common mistakes

- **Using one equation for the whole flight.** With quadratic drag, $mv' = -mg - kv^2$ is only
  right while the object rises. Drag is $-kv|v|$, so split the motion at the top.
- **Expecting a symmetric flight.** With drag, the fall is slower and lands at a lower speed
  than the launch.
- **Reaching for an integrating factor.** $mv' = mg - kv^2$ is nonlinear; separate variables
  (or use $w = v^2$ for speed against distance).
- **Wrong terminal velocity.** It is $\sqrt{mg/k}$ for quadratic drag, not $mg/k$; check units:
  $k$ is in kg/m, so $mg/k$ is in m²/s².
- **Confusing $\tanh^{-1}$ with $1/\tanh$.** The inverse function undoes $\tanh$; the reciprocal
  is $\coth$.

## Key points

- Low Reynolds number: linear (Stokes) drag. High Reynolds number: quadratic drag,
  $F = \tfrac12\rho C_dAv^2 = kv^2$. The cutoffs are rough.
- From rest: $v = v_T\tanh(gt/v_T)$ and $x = \dfrac{v_T^2}{g}\ln\cosh(gt/v_T)$, with
  $v_T = \sqrt{mg/k}$.
- Speed against distance: $v^2 = v_T^2(1 - e^{-2gx/v_T^2})$, from the substitution $w = v^2$.
- Thrown up: $t_{\text{top}} = \dfrac{v_T}{g}\tan^{-1}\dfrac{v_0}{v_T}$,
  $H = \dfrac{v_T^2}{2g}\ln\left(1 + \dfrac{v_0^2}{v_T^2}\right)$,
  $v_{\text{ret}} = \dfrac{v_0v_T}{\sqrt{v_0^2 + v_T^2}}$.
- Drag reverses at the top, so up and down are different equations.

lessons.title: Drug dosing and compartment models
lessons.body:
## From tanks to bloodstreams

Lesson 12 mentioned that the mixing model also describes medicine being cleared from the
blood. This lesson takes that seriously. **[[Pharmacokinetics]]** is the study of how the body
absorbs, distributes and eliminates a drug, and its simplest models are exactly the tanks of
Lesson 12: a dose flows in, the body mixes it, and the liver and kidneys remove it. The
questions are practical ones. How fast must an IV drip run to hold a target level? Why does
a daily pill take days to reach full effect? Why do doctors sometimes give a bigger first
dose? Every answer comes from first-order linear equations you already know how to solve.

This is a teaching model, not dosing advice. Real dosing uses measured, drug-specific values
and clinical judgment.

## The one-compartment model

The **[[one-compartment model]]** treats the body as a single well-stirred tank. Let $X(t)$ be
the amount of drug in the body (mg) and $C(t)$ its concentration in the blood (mg/L). They are
linked by the **[[volume of distribution]]** $V$:

$$C = \frac{X}{V}.$$

$V$ is an *apparent* volume: it is whatever volume makes $C = X/V$ true. A drug that soaks into
fat or muscle leaves little in the blood, so its $V$ can be far larger than the body's actual
volume.

Most drugs at normal doses are removed at a rate proportional to the amount present
(first-order elimination):

$$\frac{dX}{dt} = -kX,$$

where $k$ (per hour) is the **[[elimination rate constant]]**. Two related numbers are used
clinically. The half-life is $t_{1/2} = \ln 2/k$, as in Lesson 4. The **[[clearance]]**,
$\text{CL} = kV$ (L/h), is the volume of blood completely cleared of drug per hour, so the
elimination rate is $kX = \text{CL}\cdot C$.

These are simplifications. Many drugs need two or more compartments (blood plus slowly
equilibrating tissues), and a few, such as alcohol, are eliminated at a nearly constant rate
because the enzymes that remove them saturate. The one-compartment, first-order model is
the starting point that the others build on.

## A single injection

An IV **[[bolus]]** puts the whole dose $D$ into the blood at once, so $X(0) = D$ and

$$C(t) = \frac{D}{V}e^{-kt}.$$

On a semilog plot ($\ln C$ against $t$) this is a straight line with slope $-k$ and
intercept $\ln(D/V)$. That is how $k$ and $V$ are measured: give a known dose, take blood
samples, fit the line.

### Example 1: finding the parameters

A patient receives a 500 mg IV bolus. Blood levels are 8 mg/L at 2 hours and 4 mg/L at
6 hours. Find $k$, $V$ and the clearance.

- The level halved in 4 hours, so $t_{1/2} = 4$ h and $k = \ln 2/4 \approx 0.173$ per hour.
- Run the decay backward 2 hours from the first sample: $C(0) = 8e^{2k} = 8 \cdot 2^{1/2} \approx 11.3$ mg/L.
- $V = D/C(0) = 500/11.31 \approx 44.2$ L, and $\text{CL} = kV \approx 0.173 \times 44.2 \approx 7.66$ L/h.

## A constant infusion

An IV **[[infusion]]** delivers drug at a steady rate $R_0$ (mg/h). Now

$$\frac{dX}{dt} = R_0 - kX,$$

which is exactly the constant-volume mixing tank of Lesson 12: rate in minus rate out.
Starting from zero, with $C = X/V$,

$$C(t) = \frac{R_0}{\text{CL}}\left(1 - e^{-kt}\right).$$

The level rises to the **[[steady state]]** $C_{ss} = R_0/\text{CL}$, where elimination
balances the drip. After $n$ half-lives it has covered a fraction $1 - 2^{-n}$ of the way:
50%, 75%, 87.5%, 93.8%, 96.9% after 1 to 5 half-lives. That is the source of the rule of
thumb that a drug reaches steady state in about four to five half-lives.

Notice what controls what. The steady level depends on the rate and the clearance; the
*time* to get there depends only on the half-life. Running the drip faster raises the
plateau but doesn't get you there any sooner.

### Example 2: infusion with a loading dose

A drug has $t_{1/2} = 8$ h and $V = 40$ L. The target level is 10 mg/L.

- $k = \ln 2/8 \approx 0.0866$ per hour and $\text{CL} = kV \approx 3.47$ L/h.
- Infusion rate: $R_0 = C_{ss}\cdot\text{CL} \approx 10 \times 3.47 \approx 34.7$ mg/h.
- Time to 90% of target: $1 - e^{-kt} = 0.9$ gives $t = \ln 10/k \approx 26.6$ h, more than a day.

To reach the target at once, give a **[[loading dose]]**: a bolus $D_L = C_{ss}V = 400$ mg at
the start, together with the infusion. The equation is linear, so the two responses add
(the superposition principle): the bolus contributes $10e^{-kt}$, the infusion
$10(1 - e^{-kt})$, and the total is exactly 10 mg/L from the first minute. The infusion that
then keeps the level there is the **[[maintenance dose]]**.

## Repeated doses

Most drugs are taken as a dose $D$ every $\tau$ hours, the **[[dosing interval]]**. Treat each
dose as a bolus. Between doses the level decays by the factor $r = e^{-k\tau}$, the fraction
left after one interval. Just after dose $n$, the level is the new dose plus what remains of
the earlier ones:

$$C_n = \frac{D}{V}\left(1 + r + r^2 + \cdots + r^{n-1}\right) = \frac{D}{V}\cdot\frac{1 - r^n}{1 - r}.$$

That is a geometric series. As $n$ grows, $r^n \to 0$, and the peaks approach the
steady-state peak

$$C_{\text{peak}} = \frac{D/V}{1 - r}, \qquad C_{\text{trough}} = rC_{\text{peak}}.$$

The number $\dfrac{1}{1 - r}$ is the **[[accumulation factor]]**: how many times higher the
steady-state peak is than the first one. At steady state each dose adds exactly $D/V$, and
each interval removes exactly $D/V$.

### Example 3: a dose every half-life

A patient takes 300 mg every 6 hours. The drug has $V = 30$ L and $t_{1/2} = 6$ h.

- Each dose adds $D/V = 10$ mg/L, and $r = e^{-k\tau} = 2^{-6/6} = \tfrac12$.
- Peaks: 10, then $10 + 5 = 15$, then 17.5, 18.75, 19.375, … mg/L.
- Accumulation factor $1/(1 - \tfrac12) = 2$: the peaks approach 20 mg/L and the troughs 10 mg/L.

```plot
{"x": [0, 36], "y": [0, 25], "xLabel": "t (hours)", "yLabel": "C (mg/L)", "functions": [{"f": "10exp(-0.115525x)", "from": 0, "to": 6}, {"f": "15exp(-0.115525(x-6))", "from": 6, "to": 12}, {"f": "17.5exp(-0.115525(x-12))", "from": 12, "to": 18}, {"f": "18.75exp(-0.115525(x-18))", "from": 18, "to": 24}, {"f": "19.375exp(-0.115525(x-24))", "from": 24, "to": 30}, {"f": "19.6875exp(-0.115525(x-30))", "from": 30, "to": 36}, {"f": "20", "dashed": true, "label": "steady peak 20"}, {"f": "10", "dashed": true}], "segments": [{"from": [6, 5], "to": [6, 15]}, {"from": [12, 7.5], "to": [12, 17.5]}, {"from": [18, 8.75], "to": [18, 18.75]}, {"from": [24, 9.375], "to": [24, 19.375]}, {"from": [30, 9.6875], "to": [30, 19.6875]}], "caption": "300 mg every 6 hours with a 6-hour half-life: each dose jumps the level up 10 mg/L, and the peaks and troughs climb toward the dashed lines at 20 and 10 mg/L."}
```

A loading dose works here too: a first dose of $D/(1 - r) = 600$ mg starts the patient at the
steady-state peak. The average level at steady state is $\dfrac{D}{\text{CL}\cdot\tau}$, here
$\dfrac{300}{3.47 \times 6} \approx 14.4$ mg/L. It is a little below the midpoint of 20 and 10,
because the decay curve sags. Smaller doses given more often keep the same average with a
smaller swing between peak and trough.

## Taking a drug by mouth

A pill first dissolves in the gut and is absorbed from there into the blood: two
compartments in series, like the two tanks in Lesson 12.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Compartments for a drug taken by mouth
  accDescr: An oral dose enters the gut, which holds amount A and passes drug into the body at rate k_a times A. The body holds amount X, with concentration X over V, and eliminates drug at rate k times X.
  D["Oral dose"] --> G["Gut: amount A; absorbed at rate ka·A"]
  G --> B["Body: amount X, concentration X/V; eliminated at rate k·X"]
  B --> E["Eliminated (liver, kidneys)"]
```

Only a fraction $F$ of the dose, the **[[bioavailability]]**, ever reaches the circulation. With
absorption rate constant $k_a$:

$$A' = -k_aA,\quad A(0) = FD; \qquad X' = k_aA - kX,\quad X(0) = 0.$$

Solve the gut first: $A = FDe^{-k_at}$. Then $X' + kX = k_aFDe^{-k_at}$ is linear; with
integrating factor $e^{kt}$ and $k_a \ne k$,

$$X(t) = \frac{FDk_a}{k_a - k}\left(e^{-kt} - e^{-k_at}\right).$$

The level rises, peaks and falls. Setting $X' = 0$ gives the peak time

$$t_{\max} = \frac{\ln(k_a/k)}{k_a - k}.$$

If $k_a = k$, the formula breaks down and the solution is $X = FDk\,te^{-kt}$, the same
$te^{-t/20}$ shape as tank B in Lesson 12.

### Example 4: a tablet

A 500 mg tablet has $F = 0.8$, $k_a = 1.0$ per hour, $k = 0.2$ per hour, and $V = 50$ L. When
does the blood level peak, and how high?

- $t_{\max} = \dfrac{\ln 5}{0.8} \approx 2.01$ h.
- $C_{\max} = \dfrac{FD}{V}\cdot\dfrac{k_a}{k_a - k}\left(e^{-kt_{\max}} - e^{-k_at_{\max}}\right) = 8(1.25)(0.6687 - 0.1337) \approx 5.35$ mg/L.

Compare an IV bolus of the same 400 mg that actually reaches the blood: it would start at
8 mg/L. Slow absorption flattens and delays the peak.

## Common mistakes

- **Amount versus concentration.** Equations balance amounts ($X$, mg); blood tests measure
  concentrations ($C = X/V$, mg/L). Convert with $V$.
- **Thinking a faster drip reaches steady state sooner.** The time scale is set by the
  half-life alone; only a loading dose shortcuts it.
- **Summing the series wrong.** After $n$ doses the sum has $n$ terms, $1 + r + \cdots + r^{n-1}$,
  not $r^n$ terms or $n + 1$.
- **Forgetting bioavailability** for oral doses: only $FD$ reaches the blood.
- **Treating $V$ as a real volume.** It is an apparent volume and can exceed body volume.

## Key points

- One compartment: $X' = (\text{rate in}) - kX$, $C = X/V$, $\text{CL} = kV$, $t_{1/2} = \ln 2/k$.
- Bolus: $C = (D/V)e^{-kt}$. Infusion: $C = (R_0/\text{CL})(1 - e^{-kt})$, steady state in about
  4 to 5 half-lives; loading dose $C_{ss}V$.
- Repeated doses: $r = e^{-k\tau}$, steady peak $(D/V)/(1 - r)$, trough $r$ times the peak.
- Oral dosing is two tanks in series: $t_{\max} = \ln(k_a/k)/(k_a - k)$.

lessons.title: Autonomous equations and phase lines
lessons.body:
## Understanding without solving

The models so far all had formula solutions. Often, though, what you really want to know
is qualitative: will the population die out or level off? Will the temperature settle?
For **[[autonomous]]** equations, $y' = f(y)$, you can answer such questions from the graph
of $f$ alone, without solving. This lesson builds that tool, the phase line, and the
language of stability that runs through the rest of the course.

## Equilibria

An **[[equilibrium]]** (also called a critical point or equilibrium solution) is a value
$y^*$ with $f(y^*) = 0$. Then the constant function $y(t) = y^*$ is a solution: the system
sits there forever.

Between equilibria, $f(y)$ has a fixed sign (if $f$ is continuous). Where $f > 0$,
solutions increase; where $f < 0$, they decrease. And since $f$ and $f'$ are continuous
in typical models, uniqueness says solutions can't cross an equilibrium. So a solution
starting between two equilibria moves monotonically toward one of them.

## The phase line

A **[[phase line]]** is a vertical copy of the $y$-axis showing the equilibria as dots, with
arrows between them pointing up where $f > 0$ and down where $f < 0$. It's a compressed
slope field: since the slopes don't depend on $t$, one column says everything.

To draw it:

1. Solve $f(y) = 0$ for the equilibria.
2. Test the sign of $f$ in each interval between them.
3. Draw arrows: up for positive, down for negative.

The whole procedure, through the classification described in the next section, fits in one
chart:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Drawing and reading a phase line
  accDescr: Start with an autonomous equation y' = f(y). Solve f(y) = 0 to find the equilibria. Test the sign of f in each interval between them, and draw an up arrow where f is positive and a down arrow where it is negative. Then look at the two arrows next to each equilibrium. If both point toward it, it is asymptotically stable, a sink. If both point away, it is unstable, a source. If one points toward it and one away, it is semistable.
  A["Autonomous equation y′ = f(y)"] --> B["Solve f(y) = 0: the equilibria"]
  B --> C["Test the sign of f between equilibria"]
  C --> D["Arrow up where f is positive, down where negative"]
  D --> E{"Arrows next to an equilibrium?"}
  E -- "both toward it" --> F["Asymptotically stable (sink)"]
  E -- "both away" --> G["Unstable (source)"]
  E -- "one toward, one away" --> H["Semistable"]
```

## Stability

An equilibrium is classified by what nearby solutions do.

- **[[Asymptotically stable]]** (a **[[sink]]**): arrows on both sides point toward it. Nearby
  solutions approach it as $t \to \infty$.
- **[[Unstable]]** (a **[[source]]**): arrows on both sides point away. Nearby solutions leave.
- **[[Semistable]]**: arrows point toward it on one side and away
  on the other.

Here are all three on one phase line, for $y' = (y + 2)(y - 1)^2(y - 3)$. A filled dot marks a
sink, an open dot a source and a half-filled dot a semistable equilibrium, a common drawing
convention.

![A vertical phase line for y′ = (y + 2)(y − 1)²(y − 3). Arrows point up above y = 3, down between 1 and 3, down between −2 and 1, and up below −2. So y = 3 is unstable (a source, open dot), y = 1 is semistable (half-filled dot) and y = −2 is asymptotically stable (a sink, filled dot).](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### The derivative test

If $f'(y^*) < 0$, then $f$ goes from positive to negative across $y^*$: arrows point in
from both sides, so $y^*$ is asymptotically stable. If $f'(y^*) > 0$, it's unstable. If
$f'(y^*) = 0$, the test is inconclusive; look at signs directly.

Why does this work? Near $y^*$, $f(y) \approx f'(y^*)(y - y^*)$, so $u = y - y^*$
satisfies approximately $u' = f'(y^*)u$, whose solutions $u = u_0e^{f'(y^*)t}$ decay when
$f'(y^*) < 0$ and grow when $f'(y^*) > 0$. This **[[linearization]]** idea comes back in
Module 8 for systems.

### Example 1

Analyze $y' = y(4 - y)$.

- Equilibria: $y = 0$, $y = 4$.
- Signs: for $y < 0$, $f < 0$ (down); for $0 < y < 4$, $f > 0$ (up); for $y > 4$, $f < 0$ (down).
- $y = 0$: arrows point away (down below, up above): unstable.
  $y = 4$: arrows point toward it: asymptotically stable.
- Derivative test agrees: $f'(y) = 4 - 2y$; $f'(0) = 4 > 0$, $f'(4) = -4 < 0$.

This is the logistic equation. Any positive starting population tends to 4.

```plot
{"x": [-1.5, 5.5], "y": [-6, 5], "xLabel": "y", "yLabel": "f(y)", "functions": [{"f": "x*(4 - x)", "label": "f(y) = y(4 − y)"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 0], "open": true, "label": "0: unstable"}, {"at": [4, 0], "label": "4: stable"}], "caption": "The sign of f(y) gives the phase-line arrows: down for y < 0, up for 0 < y < 4, down for y > 4."}
```

```plot
{"x": [0, 6], "y": [-1.5, 6], "xLabel": "t", "slopeField": {"f": "y*(4 - y)", "step": 0.5}, "functions": [{"f": "4/(1 + 7exp(-4x))", "label": "y(0) = 0.5"}, {"f": "4/(1 - 0.5exp(-4x))", "from": 0.2, "label": "y(0) = 8"}, {"f": "4", "dashed": true}, {"f": "0", "dashed": true}], "caption": "Solutions of y′ = y(4 − y): y = 4 attracts, y = 0 repels."}
```

### Example 2

Analyze $y' = (y - 1)^2(y + 2)$.

- Equilibria: $y = 1$ and $y = -2$.
- Signs: $y < -2$: $(+)(-) < 0$, down. $-2 < y < 1$: $(+)(+) > 0$, up. $y > 1$: $(+)(+) > 0$, up.
- $y = -2$: down below, up above: unstable.
- $y = 1$: up below (toward it), up above (away): **[[semistable]]**. Note $f'(1) = 0$,
  so the derivative test says nothing; the squared factor is the giveaway, since it
  doesn't change sign.

### Example 3

A solution of $y' = y^3 - 9y$ starts at $y(0) = 2$. What is $\lim_{t\to\infty} y(t)$?

- $f(y) = y(y - 3)(y + 3)$; equilibria $-3, 0, 3$.
- On $(0, 3)$: try $y = 1$: $1 - 9 < 0$, so solutions decrease.
- Starting at 2, the solution decreases toward the next equilibrium below, $y = 0$.
  The limit is 0. (Check: $f'(0) = -9 < 0$, so 0 is stable.)

## Reading the shape of solutions

The phase line tells you more than limits. Since $y'' = f'(y)\,y' = f'(y)f(y)$,
solutions have inflection points where $f'(y) = 0$, that is, at the peaks and troughs of
the graph of $f$. For the logistic $y' = y(4 - y)$, $f'(y) = 0$ at $y = 2$: the S-curve
bends there, exactly halfway to the carrying capacity, as Lesson 4 found.

## Population thresholds

Some species need a minimum population to survive (mates must find each other). A model
with an **[[extinction threshold]]** $T$ and carrying capacity $K$ is

$$P' = -rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{T}\right)\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right), \qquad 0 < T < K.$$

Check the signs. For $0 < P < T$: $\left(1 - \frac PT\right) > 0$, $\left(1 - \frac PK\right) > 0$, so $P' < 0$ and the
population dies out. Between $T$ and $K$: $P' > 0$, so it grows to $K$. Above $K$: $P' < 0$.
So $0$ and $K$ are stable, and $T$ is unstable: a tipping point.

## Common mistakes

- **Using $t$.** Phase lines only work for autonomous equations; $y' = t - y$ needs a full
  slope field.
- **Reading the wrong graph.** The arrows come from the sign of $f(y)$, not from the sign
  of $y$.
- **Trusting $f'(y^*) = 0$.** That case needs a direct sign check.
- **Thinking solutions reach equilibria.** They approach as $t \to \infty$ but (with
  uniqueness) never arrive in finite time.

## Key points

- Equilibria of $y' = f(y)$ solve $f(y) = 0$; arrows up where $f > 0$, down where $f < 0$.
- Stable: arrows point in. Unstable: arrows point out. Semistable: mixed.
- Derivative test: $f'(y^*) < 0$ stable, $f'(y^*) > 0$ unstable, $= 0$ inconclusive.
- A solution moves monotonically toward the next equilibrium in the arrow's direction
  (or to $\pm\infty$).

lessons.title: Population models and bifurcations
lessons.body:
## When a parameter changes the story

Models contain parameters: a growth rate, a harvesting quota, a drug dose. Usually,
nudging a parameter nudges the answer a little. But at certain critical values, the
whole qualitative picture changes: equilibria appear, vanish, or swap stability. Such a
change is a **[[bifurcation]]**, and the critical parameter value is a
**[[bifurcation value]]**. This lesson applies last lesson's phase lines to families of
equations $y' = f(y, c)$ that depend on a parameter $c$.

## Logistic growth with harvesting

Start with a fish population following the logistic law, and suppose fishing removes $h$
tonnes per year at a constant rate:

$$P' = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) - h.$$

Equilibria solve $rP(1 - P/K) = h$. The left side is a downward parabola with maximum
value $rK/4$ at $P = K/2$ (Lesson 4). Three cases:

- $h < rK/4$: the horizontal line at height $h$ crosses the parabola twice, giving two
  equilibria $P_1 < P_2$. The lower one is unstable (a threshold), the upper one stable.
  A population above $P_1$ settles at $P_2$; below $P_1$ it collapses.
- $h = rK/4$: one equilibrium at $P = K/2$, semistable.
- $h > rK/4$: no equilibria; $P' < 0$ always and the population crashes to zero no matter
  how large it starts.

So $h^* = rK/4$, the **[[maximum sustainable yield]]**, is the bifurcation value. Fishing
slightly below it looks safe, but the threshold $P_1$ creeps up toward $K/2$; a bad year
can push the population below it and into collapse.

### Example 1

For $P' = P(1 - P/100) - h$ (thousands of fish, per year), find the equilibria when
$h = 16$ and the bifurcation value.

- Equilibria: $P - \dfrac{P^2}{100} = 16$, so $P^2 - 100P + 1600 = 0$, giving
  $P = \dfrac{100 \pm \sqrt{10000 - 6400}}{2} = \dfrac{100 \pm 60}{2}$: $P_1 = 20$, $P_2 = 80$.
- Stability: $f'(P) = 1 - \dfrac{P}{50}$; $f'(20) = 0.6 > 0$ (unstable), $f'(80) = -0.6 < 0$
  (stable).
- Bifurcation: $h^* = rK/4 = 1 \cdot 100/4 = 25$.

## Bifurcation diagrams

A **[[bifurcation diagram]]** plots the equilibria against the parameter: parameter on the
horizontal axis, equilibrium values on the vertical. Stable branches are drawn solid,
unstable ones dashed. For harvesting with $r = 1$, $K = 100$, the equilibria
$P = 50 \pm \sqrt{2500 - 100h}$ trace a parabola lying on its side, opening to the left,
that ends at $h = 25$.

```plot
{"x": [0, 30], "y": [0, 110], "xLabel": "h", "yLabel": "P*", "functions": [{"f": "50 + sqrt(2500 - 100x)", "to": 25, "label": "stable"}, {"f": "50 - sqrt(2500 - 100x)", "to": 25, "dashed": true, "label": "unstable"}], "points": [{"at": [25, 50], "label": "h* = 25"}], "caption": "Bifurcation diagram for P′ = P(1 − P/100) − h: the two equilibria merge and vanish at h = 25."}
```

This kind of bifurcation, in which two equilibria collide and annihilate, is called a
**[[saddle-node bifurcation]]**. The prototype is $y' = c + y^2$:

- $c < 0$: equilibria $\pm\sqrt{-c}$; $-\sqrt{-c}$ stable, $+\sqrt{-c}$ unstable.
- $c = 0$: one semistable equilibrium at 0.
- $c > 0$: none.

## Other standard bifurcations

**Transcritical.** Two equilibria pass through each other and exchange stability.
Prototype $y' = cy - y^2 = y(c - y)$: equilibria $0$ and $c$. For $c < 0$, $0$ is stable;
for $c > 0$, $0$ is unstable and $c$ is stable. They swap at $c = 0$. Example: in
$P' = (b - d)P - kP^2$ (births minus deaths), the extinct state $P = 0$ is stable until the
birth rate overtakes the death rate.

**Pitchfork.** One equilibrium splits into three. Prototype $y' = cy - y^3$: for $c \le 0$
only $y = 0$ (stable); for $c > 0$, $y = 0$ becomes unstable and two new stable equilibria
$\pm\sqrt{c}$ appear. The diagram looks like a pitchfork.

Side by side, the three bifurcation diagrams look like this (parameter $c$ across, equilibria
$y^*$ up; solid stable, dashed unstable):

![Three bifurcation diagrams. Saddle-node, y′ = c + y²: for c < 0 a stable lower branch and an unstable upper branch, a sideways parabola that ends at the origin; nothing for c > 0. Transcritical, y′ = cy − y²: the lines y* = 0 and y* = c cross at the origin and swap stability, so y* = 0 is stable for c < 0 and the line y* = c is stable for c > 0. Pitchfork, y′ = cy − y³: y* = 0 is stable for c < 0 and unstable for c > 0, where two stable branches ±√c open out like the tines of a fork.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

To name a bifurcation, watch what the equilibria do as the parameter crosses its critical
value:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Naming a bifurcation
  accDescr: As the parameter crosses the bifurcation value, compare the equilibria just before and just after. If two equilibria collide and disappear, it is a saddle-node bifurcation, with prototype y' = c + y squared. If two equilibria pass through each other and swap stability, it is a transcritical bifurcation, with prototype y' = cy − y squared. If one equilibrium splits into three, it is a pitchfork bifurcation, with prototype y' = cy − y cubed.
  A["The parameter crosses its critical value"] --> B{"What do the equilibria do?"}
  B -- "two collide and vanish" --> C["Saddle-node: y′ = c + y²"]
  B -- "two cross and swap stability" --> D["Transcritical: y′ = cy − y²"]
  B -- "one splits into three" --> E["Pitchfork: y′ = cy − y³"]
```

### Example 2

Find the bifurcation value and describe the change for $y' = y^2 - 4y + c$.

- Equilibria: $y = \dfrac{4 \pm \sqrt{16 - 4c}}{2} = 2 \pm \sqrt{4 - c}$.
- For $c < 4$: two equilibria. $f'(y) = 2y - 4$, so $2 + \sqrt{4 - c}$ is unstable
  ($f' > 0$) and $2 - \sqrt{4 - c}$ is stable.
- At $c = 4$: one equilibrium $y = 2$ (semistable). For $c > 4$: none, and every solution
  increases (and in fact blows up).
- Bifurcation value $c = 4$; it's a saddle-node bifurcation.

### Example 3

For $y' = cy - y^3$, classify the equilibria when $c = 9$.

- $y(9 - y^2) = 0$ gives $y = 0, \pm 3$.
- $f'(y) = 9 - 3y^2$: $f'(0) = 9 > 0$ unstable; $f'(\pm3) = 9 - 27 = -18 < 0$ stable.
- Solutions starting at any positive value tend to 3; negative ones tend to $-3$.

## A general recipe

A bifurcation can only happen where an equilibrium stops being "robust", that is where
both

$$f(y, c) = 0 \quad\text{and}\quad \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(y, c) = 0.$$

Solving these two equations together locates candidate bifurcation points. For harvesting:
$f = P - P^2/100 - h$ and $f_P = 1 - P/50 = 0$ give $P = 50$, then $h = 50 - 25 = 25$.

## Common mistakes

- **Plotting the wrong axes.** In a bifurcation diagram the parameter is horizontal.
- **Forgetting stability changes.** Count equilibria *and* check which are stable.
- **Assuming harvesting at the maximum sustainable yield is safe.** At $h = rK/4$ the
  equilibrium is semistable; any downward disturbance leads to collapse.
- **Mislabeling the types.** Two equilibria vanishing is saddle-node; exchanging stability
  is transcritical; one splitting into three is pitchfork.

## Key points

- A bifurcation is a qualitative change in the phase line as a parameter crosses a
  critical value.
- Logistic harvesting $P' = rP(1 - P/K) - h$ has two equilibria for $h < rK/4$, none for
  $h > rK/4$.
- Locate bifurcations by solving $f = 0$ and $f_y = 0$ together.
- Prototypes: saddle-node $c + y^2$, transcritical $cy - y^2$, pitchfork $cy - y^3$.

lessons.title: Error and the improved Euler method
lessons.body:
## Why we need better methods

Euler's method (Lesson 5) is simple and honest, but slow to converge: to get one more
correct digit you need about ten times as many steps. For a model run over years of
simulated time, or a spacecraft trajectory, that's too expensive. This lesson explains
*why* Euler's error behaves as it does and builds the first improvement, the improved
Euler method (also called **[[Heun's method]]**).

## Two kinds of error

Ignoring round-off, there are two errors to keep apart.

- **[[Local truncation error]]**: the error made in a *single* step, assuming you started
  that step exactly on the true solution.
- **[[Global error]]**: the total error at the end, $y(t_N) - y_N$, after errors from all
  steps have accumulated and propagated.

### Euler's local error

Taylor's theorem says the true solution satisfies

$$y(t + h) = y(t) + h\,y'(t) + \frac{h^2}{2}y''(\xi)$$

for some $\xi$ between $t$ and $t + h$. Euler's step keeps the first two terms and
throws away the third, so the local error is about $\dfrac{h^2}{2}y''$: proportional to
$h^2$.

### From local to global

To cross a fixed interval of length $L$ takes $N = L/h$ steps. If each step adds error of
order $h^2$, the total is roughly $N \cdot h^2 = Lh$, proportional to $h$. That's why
halving $h$ halved the error in Lesson 5. A method whose global error is proportional to
$h^p$ is said to have **[[order]]** $p$. Euler's method has order 1.

### Example 1

For $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$, compare Euler estimates of $y(1) = e \approx 2.718282$.

| $h$ | Euler estimate $(1 + h)^{1/h}$ | Error | Error ÷ $h$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1 | 2.593742 | 0.124539 | 1.245 |
| 0.05 | 2.653298 | 0.064984 | 1.300 |
| 0.025 | 2.685064 | 0.033218 | 1.329 |

Error ÷ $h$ settles near a constant (it tends to $e/2 \approx 1.36$): the error is
proportional to $h$, as predicted.

## The improved Euler method

Euler's method uses the slope at the *start* of the step for the whole step. If the
slope changes over the step, that's biased. A better idea is to average the slopes at
the start and the end. We don't know the end yet, but we can estimate it with an Euler
step. That gives a **[[predictor-corrector]]** scheme:

$$\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= f(t_n, y_n) &&\text{slope at the start}\\
k_2 &= f(t_n + h,\ y_n + hk_1) &&\text{slope at the Euler-predicted end}\\
y_{n+1} &= y_n + \frac{h}{2}(k_1 + k_2) &&\text{step with the average slope}
\end{aligned}$$

It's the trapezoid rule applied to $y(t + h) = y(t) + \int_t^{t+h} f\,ds$, just as
Euler's method is the left-endpoint rule. Its local error is proportional to $h^3$ and
its global error to $h^2$: it is a **[[second-order method]]**. Halving $h$ cuts the error by
about a factor of 4.

The picture shows one step for $y' = y$ from $(t_n, y_n) = (0, 1)$ with a deliberately large
$h = 1$. Euler's step follows the starting slope $k_1 = 1$ and lands at 2, well below the
curve. The slope there is $k_2 = 2$. The average slope $1.5$ carries the step to $2.5$, much
closer to the true $e \approx 2.718$.

![One improved Euler step. From the starting point, a dashed line with slope k₁ reaches the Euler prediction at t + h. A short dashed segment there shows the slope k₂. A solid line with the average slope (k₁ + k₂)/2 from the starting point ends at the improved Euler value, which lies much closer to the curved true solution than the Euler prediction does.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

As a procedure, each step is four moves:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: One step of the improved Euler method
  accDescr: From the current point t_n, y_n, compute the starting slope k1 = f(t_n, y_n). Use it for a trial Euler step to predict y at t_n + h. Compute the slope k2 at that predicted point. Then step from y_n with the average of k1 and k2 to get y_(n+1).
  A["Current point (tₙ, yₙ)"] --> B["Slope at the start: k₁ = f(tₙ, yₙ)"]
  B --> C["Predict: yₙ + h·k₁ at tₙ + h"]
  C --> D["Slope at the prediction: k₂"]
  D --> E["Correct: yₙ₊₁ = yₙ + (h/2)(k₁ + k₂)"]
```

### Example 2

Use improved Euler with $h = 0.5$ for $y' = t + y$, $y(0) = 1$, to estimate $y(1)$.
(Exact: $y = 2e^t - t - 1$, so $y(1) \approx 3.436564$.)

Step 1 (from $t = 0$, $y = 1$):

- $k_1 = 0 + 1 = 1$.
- Predicted end: $y = 1 + 0.5(1) = 1.5$ at $t = 0.5$; $k_2 = 0.5 + 1.5 = 2$.
- $y_1 = 1 + 0.25(1 + 2) = 1.75$.

Step 2 (from $t = 0.5$, $y = 1.75$):

- $k_1 = 0.5 + 1.75 = 2.25$.
- Predicted end: $1.75 + 0.5(2.25) = 2.875$ at $t = 1$; $k_2 = 1 + 2.875 = 3.875$.
- $y_2 = 1.75 + 0.25(2.25 + 3.875) = 1.75 + 1.53125 = 3.28125$.

The error is $3.436564 - 3.28125 \approx 0.155$, compared with 0.937 for Euler with the same
step size. Each step costs two evaluations of $f$ instead of one, but the accuracy gain is
far larger.

### Example 3

One step of improved Euler for $y' = -2ty$, $y(0) = 1$, with $h = 0.1$.

- $k_1 = -2(0)(1) = 0$.
- Predicted: $y = 1 + 0.1(0) = 1$ at $t = 0.1$; $k_2 = -2(0.1)(1) = -0.2$.
- $y_1 = 1 + 0.05(0 - 0.2) = 0.99$.
- Exact: $e^{-0.01} \approx 0.990050$. Error about $5 \times 10^{-5}$. Euler would have
  given $y_1 = 1$, error $0.01$.

## Estimating error without the exact answer

In practice you don't know the true solution. A standard trick: compute with step $h$
and with step $h/2$. For a method of order $p$, the error with $h/2$ is about $1/2^p$ of
the error with $h$, so the difference between the two answers reveals roughly how big
the error is. Software uses this idea to choose step sizes automatically (adaptive
methods), taking small steps where the solution changes quickly and large ones where it's
smooth.

## Round-off error

Computers carry finitely many digits, so each arithmetic step adds a tiny
**[[round-off error]]**. With extremely small $h$ there are so many steps that round-off
can start to dominate. In practice, a higher-order method with a moderate step beats a
low-order method with a microscopic one.

## Common mistakes

- **Using $t_n$ in $k_2$.** The second slope is evaluated at $t_n + h$, the end of the step.
- **Using $h$ instead of $h/2$** in the final update; the average slope is $(k_1 + k_2)/2$.
- **Confusing local and global order.** Euler: local $h^2$, global $h$. Improved Euler:
  local $h^3$, global $h^2$.

## Key points

- Local error is per step; global error accumulates over $L/h$ steps, so it is one power
  of $h$ lower.
- Euler's method is first order: error $\propto h$.
- Improved Euler (Heun): $k_1 = f(t_n, y_n)$, $k_2 = f(t_n + h, y_n + hk_1)$,
  $y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac h2(k_1 + k_2)$; second order, error $\propto h^2$.

lessons.title: Runge–Kutta methods
lessons.body:
## The standard tool

Improved Euler averaged two slopes and gained an order of accuracy. Sampling more slopes
cleverly gains more. The **[[Runge–Kutta methods]]** are a family built on this idea, and the
classical fourth-order member, usually called **[[RK4]]**, is the default numerical method in
countless programs. It's accurate, simple to code, and needs no derivatives of $f$ beyond
evaluating $f$ itself.

## The RK4 formulas

To advance $y' = f(t, y)$ from $(t_n, y_n)$ by a step $h$:

$$\begin{aligned}
k_1 &= f(t_n,\ y_n)\\
k_2 &= f\!\left(t_n + \tfrac h2,\ y_n + \tfrac h2 k_1\right)\\
k_3 &= f\!\left(t_n + \tfrac h2,\ y_n + \tfrac h2 k_2\right)\\
k_4 &= f(t_n + h,\ y_n + hk_3)\\
y_{n+1} &= y_n + \frac h6\left(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4\right)
\end{aligned}$$

Read it as four slope samples:

- $k_1$: the slope at the start (Euler's slope).
- $k_2$: the slope at the midpoint, reached by following $k_1$ for half a step.
- $k_3$: the slope at the midpoint again, this time reached using the better slope $k_2$.
- $k_4$: the slope at the end, reached using $k_3$ for a full step.

Here is where those four slopes are sampled for $y' = y$ from $(0, 1)$ with $h = 1$ (a large
step, to spread the points out). Each short bar shows the slope at a sample point:

![The four RK4 sample points for y′ = y starting at (0, 1) with h = 1. k₁ is sampled at the start. k₂ is sampled at the midpoint t + h/2, at height 1.5, reached by following k₁. k₃ is sampled at the midpoint again, at height 1.75, reached by following k₂. k₄ is sampled at the end t + h, at height 2.75, reached by following k₃. The true solution curve passes close to the last point.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The final slope is a weighted average with weights $1, 2, 2, 1$ (dividing by 6). If $f$
depends only on $t$, then $k_2 = k_3$ and the update becomes
$\frac{h}{6}\left(f(t_n) + 4f(t_n + \tfrac h2) + f(t_n + h)\right)$, which is exactly
**[[Simpson's rule]]** for $\int f\,dt$. That connection explains the weights.

RK4 has local error proportional to $h^5$ and global error proportional to $h^4$: halving
$h$ cuts the error by about 16. It costs four evaluations of $f$ per step.

### Example 1

Use one RK4 step with $h = 0.5$ for $y' = t + y$, $y(0) = 1$, then a second, to estimate
$y(1)$.

Step 1 from $(0, 1)$:

- $k_1 = 0 + 1 = 1$
- $k_2 = f(0.25,\ 1 + 0.25(1)) = 0.25 + 1.25 = 1.5$
- $k_3 = f(0.25,\ 1 + 0.25(1.5)) = 0.25 + 1.375 = 1.625$
- $k_4 = f(0.5,\ 1 + 0.5(1.625)) = 0.5 + 1.8125 = 2.3125$
- $y_1 = 1 + \dfrac{0.5}{6}(1 + 3 + 3.25 + 2.3125) = 1 + \dfrac{0.5}{6}(9.5625) = 1.796875$

Step 2 from $(0.5, 1.796875)$ (same pattern) gives $y_2 \approx 3.434692$.

The exact value is $3.436564$, so the error is about 0.0019, using just two steps.
Compare: Euler 0.937, improved Euler 0.155, RK4 0.0019 with the same $h = 0.5$.

### Example 2

One RK4 step with $h = 0.2$ for $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$:

- $k_1 = 1$
- $k_2 = 1 + 0.1(1) = 1.1$
- $k_3 = 1 + 0.1(1.1) = 1.11$
- $k_4 = 1 + 0.2(1.11) = 1.222$
- $y_1 = 1 + \dfrac{0.2}{6}(1 + 2.2 + 2.22 + 1.222) = 1 + \dfrac{0.2}{6}(6.642) = 1.2214$

Exact: $e^{0.2} = 1.221403$. Multiply out and you'll find that one RK4 step for $y' = y$
multiplies by $1 + h + \dfrac{h^2}{2} + \dfrac{h^3}{6} + \dfrac{h^4}{24}$, the first five
terms of the Taylor series of $e^h$. That's what "fourth order" means.

## Comparing the methods

For $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$ on $[0, 1]$ (exact $e \approx 2.718282$):

| Method | $h$ | Evaluations of $f$ | Estimate | Error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Euler | 0.1 | 10 | 2.593742 | $1.2 \times 10^{-1}$ |
| Improved Euler | 0.1 | 20 | 2.714081 | $4.2 \times 10^{-3}$ |
| RK4 | 0.2 | 20 | 2.718251 | $3.1 \times 10^{-5}$ |
| RK4 | 0.1 | 40 | 2.718280 | $2.1 \times 10^{-6}$ |

For the same work (20 evaluations), RK4 is over 100 times more accurate than improved
Euler. Halving its step from 0.2 to 0.1 cut the error by about 15, close to the predicted 16.

```plot
{"x": [-3, 0], "y": [-6, 0], "xLabel": "log₁₀ h", "yLabel": "log₁₀ error", "functions": [{"f": "x + 0.13", "label": "Euler (slope 1)"}, {"f": "2x - 0.38", "label": "improved Euler (slope 2)"}, {"f": "4x - 1.72", "label": "RK4 (slope 4)"}], "caption": "On log–log axes, error against step size is a line whose slope is the order of the method (approximate, for y′ = y on [0, 1])."}
```

## Systems and higher order

All these methods extend directly to systems $\mathbf{y}' = \mathbf{f}(t, \mathbf{y})$:
treat $y$ and each $k_i$ as vectors. Since any higher-order equation can be rewritten as a
first-order system (Module 8), RK4 handles them too. For example $y'' = -y$ becomes
$y_1' = y_2$, $y_2' = -y_1$.

## When numerical methods struggle

- **Blow-up.** Near a vertical asymptote, as with $y' = y^2$, no fixed step size works;
  the solution changes too fast.
- **Stiff equations.** If a solution has a very fast-decaying component, such as
  $y' = -1000(y - \cos t)$, explicit methods like Euler and RK4 need tiny steps just to
  stay stable, even when the solution itself is smooth. Euler's method on $y' = -\lambda y$
  multiplies by $1 - h\lambda$ each step; if $h\lambda > 2$ that factor has size more than 1
  and the numbers explode. Special implicit methods exist for stiff problems.

A rough guide to choosing a method (the two optional honors lessons after this one cover the
stiff and adaptive branches):

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Choosing a numerical method
  accDescr: Start from the problem. First ask whether it is stiff, meaning a fast-decaying part forces explicit methods to take tiny steps. If yes, use an implicit method designed for stiff problems. If no, ask whether the solution changes much faster in some places than in others. If yes, use an adaptive Runge–Kutta solver that varies the step size. If no, a fixed-step RK4 works well.
  A["Need a numerical solution"] --> B{"Stiff? A fast-decaying part forces tiny steps"}
  B -- "yes" --> C["Implicit method for stiff problems"]
  B -- "no" --> D{"Much faster change in some places?"}
  D -- "yes" --> E["Adaptive Runge–Kutta (varies h)"]
  D -- "no" --> F["Fixed-step RK4"]
```

## Common mistakes

- **Wrong $t$ arguments.** $k_2$ and $k_3$ use $t_n + h/2$; $k_4$ uses $t_n + h$.
- **Wrong $y$ arguments.** $k_3$ uses $y_n + \tfrac h2 k_2$ (not $k_1$); $k_4$ uses
  $y_n + hk_3$ (full step).
- **Forgetting the weights.** The average is $(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4)/6$.
- **Rounding the $k$'s.** Keep full precision through the step.

## Key points

- RK4: four slopes $k_1$ to $k_4$, weighted $1, 2, 2, 1$ over 6.
- Global error $\propto h^4$; halving $h$ cuts error by about 16.
- Order of a method = slope of log(error) against log($h$).
- The same formulas work for systems; stiff problems need special methods.

lessons.title: Harvesting policies and resilience
lessons.body:
Lesson 15 modeled a fishery that removes a fixed catch $h$ every year and found a
bifurcation: above the maximum sustainable yield $rK/4$ the population crashes. That lesson
left two questions open. Is a fixed catch the only way to manage a harvest? And can you tell
that a system is close to a tipping point *before* it tips? This lesson answers both with the
tools of Lesson 14: equilibria, phase lines and the derivative $f'(y^*)$.

The models here are deliberately simple. Real fisheries have age structure, random good and
bad years, uncertain parameters and economics. Treat the conclusions as the qualitative
lessons that the simple models teach, not as management rules.

## Two harvesting policies

Start from logistic growth $P' = rP(1 - P/K)$ and subtract the catch.

- **[[Constant-quota harvesting]]** removes a fixed amount $h$ per unit time, however many fish
  there are: $P' = rP(1 - P/K) - h$. This is Lesson 15's model.
- **[[Constant-effort harvesting]]** keeps the fishing effort fixed (the same fleet, fishing the
  same number of days), so the catch is proportional to the stock: when fish are plentiful the
  nets fill faster. The model is
  $$P' = rP\left(1 - \frac{P}{K}\right) - EP,$$
  where the effort $E$ is a per-capita rate (units 1/time): the fraction of the stock caught per
  unit time. Note the different units: $h$ is an amount per year, $E$ is "per year".

## Constant effort is still logistic

Collect the terms that are linear in $P$:

$$P' = (r - E)P - \frac{r}{K}P^2 = (r - E)P\left(1 - \frac{P}{K(1 - E/r)}\right).$$

For $E < r$ this is a logistic equation with growth rate $r - E$ and carrying capacity
$K(1 - E/r)$. So everything from Lesson 4 applies, including the solution formula. The
equilibria are $P = 0$ and

$$P^* = K\left(1 - \frac{E}{r}\right).$$

With $f(P) = (r - E)P - \frac rK P^2$, the derivative is $f'(P) = (r - E) - \frac{2r}{K}P$, so

- $f'(0) = r - E$: unstable when $E < r$, stable when $E > r$;
- $f'(P^*) = (r - E) - 2(r - E) = -(r - E)$: stable when $E < r$.

At $E = r$ the two equilibria meet at 0 and swap stability. That is a transcritical
bifurcation (Lesson 15), not a saddle-node. Push effort past $r$ and the stock declines to
zero, but it does so gradually as $E$ grows: there is no sudden cliff of the kind the quota
model has.

```plot
{"x": [0, 1.5], "y": [-10, 110], "xLabel": "effort E", "yLabel": "P*", "functions": [{"f": "100(1 - x)", "to": 1}, {"f": "0", "to": 1, "dashed": true}, {"f": "0", "from": 1}], "points": [{"at": [1, 0]}], "labels": [{"at": [0.62, 62], "text": "P* = K(1 − E/r)"}, {"at": [1.12, 12], "text": "E = r"}], "caption": "Bifurcation diagram for constant effort with r = 1, K = 100: solid branches are stable, dashed unstable. The positive equilibrium shrinks steadily and meets P = 0 at E = r (transcritical)."}
```

## Sustainable yield

At the stable equilibrium the catch per unit time is constant. This **[[sustainable yield]]** is

$$Y(E) = E\,P^* = EK\left(1 - \frac Er\right).$$

As a function of $E$ it is a downward parabola with roots $E = 0$ and $E = r$, so its maximum
is at $E = r/2$:

$$Y_{\max} = \frac r2 \cdot K \cdot \frac12 = \frac{rK}{4}, \qquad P^* = \frac K2.$$

That is the same maximum sustainable yield as the quota model, reached at the same stock
$K/2$. The difference is stability. With a quota at $h = rK/4$ the equilibrium is
semistable, and any dip below $K/2$ starts a collapse (Lesson 15). With effort $E = r/2$ the
equilibrium has $f'(P^*) = -r/2 < 0$: it is a genuine sink, and the stock returns after a
dip.

```plot
{"x": [0, 1.2], "y": [0, 30], "xLabel": "effort E", "yLabel": "yield Y", "functions": [{"f": "100x(1 - x)", "to": 1}], "labels": [{"at": [0.9, 22], "text": "Y = EK(1 − E/r)"}], "points": [{"at": [0.5, 25], "label": "MSY: E = r/2"}], "caption": "Sustainable yield against effort for r = 1, K = 100. Beyond E = r/2, more effort catches less."}
```

### Example 1

A stock has $r = 0.8$ per year and $K = 500$ tonnes and is fished with constant effort
$E = 0.3$ per year. Find the equilibrium stock, the sustainable yield, and the effort for
maximum sustainable yield. What happens if effort is doubled to $0.6$?

- Equilibrium: $P^* = 500(1 - 0.3/0.8) = 500(0.625) = 312.5$ tonnes. Since $E < r$, it is stable.
- Yield: $Y = 0.3 \times 312.5 = 93.75$ tonnes per year.
- Maximum: $E = r/2 = 0.4$, giving $Y = rK/4 = 100$ tonnes per year at $P^* = 250$.
- Doubling the effort: $P^* = 500(1 - 0.6/0.8) = 125$ and $Y = 0.6 \times 125 = 75$ tonnes
  per year. Twice the effort catches *less*, from a much smaller stock. Past $r/2$ the extra
  effort removes fish faster than the smaller stock can replace them.

## Resilience and return time

Both policies can give the same yield. To compare them, ask how quickly the stock recovers
after a bad year. Near a stable equilibrium, Lesson 14's linearization says $u = P - P^*$
obeys $u' \approx f'(P^*)\,u$, so a small disturbance shrinks like $u_0 e^{f'(P^*)t}$. Define the
**[[return time]]**

$$T_R = \frac{1}{\lvert f'(P^*)\rvert},$$

the time for a small disturbance to shrink by a factor of $e \approx 2.7$. A short return time
means high **[[resilience]]** in the sense used here: the system bounces back quickly. (Ecologists
use "resilience" in more than one way; another meaning is how large a disturbance a system can
absorb without switching to a different state. Both ideas appear below.)

- Effort: $f'(P^*) = -(r - E)$, so $T_R = \dfrac{1}{r - E}$.
- Quota with $h < rK/4$: the stable equilibrium is $P_2 = \dfrac K2(1 + s)$ with
  $s = \sqrt{1 - 4h/(rK)}$, and $f'(P_2) = r - \dfrac{2r}{K}P_2 = -rs$. So
  $$T_R = \frac{1}{r\sqrt{1 - 4h/(rK)}}.$$

### Example 2

For the quota model with $r = 1$ and $K = 100$, compute the equilibria and return time for
several quotas.

| Quota $h$ | Threshold $P_1$ | Stable $P_2$ | $f'(P_2)$ | Return time $T_R$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 0 | 100 | $-1$ | 1 |
| 16 | 20 | 80 | $-0.6$ | 1.67 |
| 21 | 30 | 70 | $-0.4$ | 2.5 |
| 24 | 40 | 60 | $-0.2$ | 5 |
| 24.75 | 45 | 55 | $-0.1$ | 10 |

For example, at $h = 24$: $P = 50 \pm \sqrt{2500 - 2400} = 50 \pm 10$, and
$f'(60) = 1 - 60/50 = -0.2$, so $T_R = 5$ years. Two things get worse together as $h$ rises
toward 25. The safety margin $P_2 - P_1$ (how far the stock can fall before it can no longer
recover) shrinks from 100 to 10, and the return time grows without bound.

```plot
{"x": [0, 30], "y": [0, 12], "xLabel": "quota h", "yLabel": "return time T_R", "functions": [{"f": "1/sqrt(1 - x/25)", "to": 24.9}], "segments": [{"from": [25, 0], "to": [25, 12], "dashed": true}], "labels": [{"at": [12, 4], "text": "T_R = 1/√(1 − h/25)"}, {"at": [22.5, 10], "text": "h = 25"}], "caption": "Return time for the quota model with r = 1, K = 100. It blows up as the quota approaches the bifurcation value 25."}
```

## Critical slowing down

The growing return time is not special to fish. At a saddle-node bifurcation, $f = 0$ and
$f_y = 0$ hold together (Lesson 15's recipe), so as the parameter approaches its critical
value, $f'(y^*)$ at the surviving stable equilibrium tends to 0 and the return time tends to
infinity. This is called **[[critical slowing down]]**: just before a tipping point, the system
recovers from small knocks more and more slowly. (The same happens as $E \to r$ in the effort
model, where $T_R = 1/(r - E)$.)

Researchers in ecology, climate science and other fields have proposed using this as an
**[[early-warning signal]]**: if recovery is getting slower, or if random fluctuations in data are
getting larger and longer-lasting, the system may be nearing a tipping point. This is an
active research area, and such signals are not foolproof: some abrupt changes give no warning,
and noisy data can give false alarms.

### Example 3

With $r = 1$ and $K = 100$, compare a quota $h = 24$ with an effort $E = 0.4$. Both settle at
$P^* = 60$ and give the same yield: $0.4 \times 60 = 24$. Now a bad winter drops the stock to
35. What happens under each policy?

**Quota.** Factor the right side: $P - \dfrac{P^2}{100} - 24 = -\dfrac{(P - 40)(P - 60)}{100}$.
The threshold is $P_1 = 40$, and at $P = 35$ the rate is $-\dfrac{(-5)(-25)}{100} = -1.25$: the
stock keeps falling. Separating variables and using partial fractions,

$$t = \int_{35}^{0} \frac{-100\,dP}{(P - 40)(P - 60)} = -5\ln\left\lvert\frac{P - 60}{P - 40}\right\rvert\,\Bigg|_{35}^{0} = -5(\ln 1.5 - \ln 5) = 5\ln\frac{10}{3} \approx 6.0,$$

so the stock is gone in about 6 years unless the quota is cut.

**Effort.** Now $P' = 0.6P\left(1 - \dfrac{P}{60}\right)$, a logistic equation. At $P = 35$,
$P' = 0.6 \cdot 35 \cdot \tfrac{25}{60} = 8.75 > 0$: the stock grows back. The solution is
$P(t) = \dfrac{60}{1 + \tfrac57 e^{-0.6t}}$, which is back above 59 after about 6.2 years, and
the return time is $T_R = 1/0.6 \approx 1.7$ years.

The reason is feedback. Under constant effort, a smaller stock automatically means a smaller
catch, which helps the stock recover. A fixed quota takes the same amount however few fish are
left, which pushes a weakened stock down further. (Real effort-based management has its own
problems; for example, better boats and gear raise the effective effort over time.)

## Common mistakes

- **Treating $E$ like $h$.** Effort is a per-capita rate; the catch is $EP$, which changes as
  $P$ changes.
- **Equating same yield with same safety.** Example 3 has equal yields and opposite fates.
- **Using the return time for a large shock.** $T_R$ comes from linearization and describes
  small disturbances. A large drop can cross a threshold, and then no return time applies.
- **Forgetting the absolute value.** $T_R = 1/\lvert f'(P^*)\rvert$ only makes sense at a stable
  equilibrium, where $f'(P^*) < 0$.
- **Calling every bifurcation a cliff.** The quota model collapses suddenly at a saddle-node; the
  effort model declines gradually through a transcritical bifurcation.

## Key points

- Constant effort: $P' = rP(1 - P/K) - EP$ is logistic with rate $r - E$ and capacity
  $K(1 - E/r)$; transcritical bifurcation at $E = r$.
- Sustainable yield $Y(E) = EK(1 - E/r)$ peaks at $E = r/2$ with $Y = rK/4$, the same MSY as the
  quota model, but at a stable equilibrium.
- Return time $T_R = 1/\lvert f'(P^*)\rvert$: effort gives $1/(r - E)$; quota gives
  $1/\big(r\sqrt{1 - 4h/(rK)}\big)$.
- Near a saddle-node, $f'(y^*) \to 0$, so recovery slows (critical slowing down), a proposed
  early-warning signal.

lessons.title: Stiff equations and implicit methods
lessons.body:
Lesson 17 ended with a warning: on an equation like $y' = -1000(y - \cos t)$, Euler's method
and even RK4 need absurdly small steps, although the solution itself is smooth. This lesson
explains why, using one simple equation to measure the stability of any method, and builds
the cure: **[[implicit methods]]**, which pay more per step but can take far larger steps.

## The test equation

To see whether a method keeps errors under control, apply it to the **[[test equation]]**

$$y' = \lambda y, \qquad \lambda < 0,$$

whose solutions $y_0e^{\lambda t}$ decay to 0. A sensible method should produce numbers that
decay too. One Euler step gives $y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_n = (1 + h\lambda)y_n$. Write
$z = h\lambda$. Every one-step method we have met turns into the same pattern,
$y_{n+1} = R(z)\,y_n$, where $R$ is the method's **[[stability function]]**:

| Method | $R(z)$ |
|---|---|
| Euler | $1 + z$ |
| Improved Euler (Heun) | $1 + z + \dfrac{z^2}{2}$ |
| RK4 | $1 + z + \dfrac{z^2}{2} + \dfrac{z^3}{6} + \dfrac{z^4}{24}$ |

(Lesson 17 found the RK4 line: the first five terms of $e^z$.) After $n$ steps,
$y_n = R(z)^n y_0$, so the numbers decay exactly when $\lvert R(z)\rvert < 1$. The set of $z$ with
$\lvert R(z)\rvert \le 1$ is the method's **[[region of absolute stability]]**.

Why should one linear equation tell us about all equations? Near any solution, a small error
$e$ evolves approximately like $e' = \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}\,e$ (the linearization idea
of Lesson 14), so $\lambda = \partial f/\partial y$ plays the role of the decay rate. If
$h\,\partial f/\partial y$ lies outside the stability region, errors get amplified every step.
This is a guide, not a theorem, for nonlinear problems. For systems, $\lambda$ runs over the
eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix (Module 8), which can be complex; that is why the regions are
drawn in the complex plane.

## Step-size limits for explicit methods

For real $\lambda < 0$, Euler's method needs $-1 \le 1 + h\lambda \le 1$, that is

$$h \le \frac{2}{\lvert\lambda\rvert}.$$

For improved Euler, $1 + z + z^2/2 = \tfrac12\big((1 + z)^2 + 1\big)$ is never below $\tfrac12$,
and it is at most 1 exactly when $-2 \le z \le 0$: the same limit $h \le 2/\lvert\lambda\rvert$. For RK4
the real interval is about $-2.785 \le z \le 0$, so $h \le 2.785/\lvert\lambda\rvert$. In every
**[[explicit method]]** of this kind (one where $y_{n+1}$ is computed directly from known values),
$R$ is a polynomial, and a polynomial grows without bound, so the stability region is always
bounded: a large enough $\lvert z\rvert$ is unstable.

### Example 1

For $y' = -50y$, find the largest stable step for Euler's method and for RK4, and the
smallest number of Euler steps needed on $0 \le t \le 10$.

- Euler: $h \le 2/50 = 0.04$.
- RK4: $h \le 2.785/50 \approx 0.0557$.
- Euler on $[0, 10]$: at least $10/0.04 = 250$ steps, even though $e^{-50t}$ is
  below $10^{-20}$ after $t = 1$ and there is nothing left to follow.

## What makes an equation stiff

Take $y' = -1000(y - \cos t)$, $y(0) = 0$. Solving it as a linear equation (Lesson 8) gives

$$y = \frac{10^6\cos t + 1000\sin t}{10^6 + 1} - \frac{10^6}{10^6 + 1}e^{-1000t}.$$

The exponential term dies within a few thousandths of a second; after that $y$ is
practically $\cos t$, a slow, smooth curve. Accuracy alone would allow a step like $h = 0.05$.
But $\partial f/\partial y = -1000$, so Euler's method is stable only for $h \le 0.002$:
5,000 steps to reach $t = 10$. With $h = 0.1$, $z = -100$ and $R(z) = -99$, so any error is
multiplied by $-99$ every step. Starting from $y_0 = 0$, Euler gives
$y_1 = 100$, $y_2 \approx -9800$, $y_3 \approx 970{,}000$.

An equation like this is a **[[stiff equation]]**: stability, not accuracy, is what limits the step
size of explicit methods. Stiffness usually comes from a fast-decaying component sitting
alongside the slow behavior you actually care about, as in chemical reactions with very fast
and very slow steps, or circuits with very different time constants. There is no single
agreed precise definition; the working definition above is the useful one. (The word comes
from 1950s work on chemical reaction rates.)

## Implicit methods

Euler's method is the left-endpoint rule: it uses the slope at the start of the step. Using the
slope at the *end* gives the **[[backward Euler method]]**:

$$y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,f(t_{n+1},\ y_{n+1}).$$

The unknown $y_{n+1}$ appears on both sides, so each step means solving an equation. That makes
it an **[[implicit method]]**. On the test equation:

$$y_{n+1} = y_n + h\lambda y_{n+1} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad y_{n+1} = \frac{1}{1 - z}\,y_n, \qquad R(z) = \frac{1}{1 - z}.$$

If $\operatorname{Re} z < 0$, then $\lvert 1 - z\rvert > 1$ and $\lvert R(z)\rvert < 1$: backward Euler damps every
decaying mode, for every step size. A method whose stability region contains the whole left
half-plane is called **[[A-stable]]**. Backward Euler is only first order, like Euler, so its
accuracy is no better; what it gains is stability.

Averaging the two endpoint slopes gives the **[[trapezoidal method]]**,

$$y_{n+1} = y_n + \frac h2\Big(f(t_n, y_n) + f(t_{n+1}, y_{n+1})\Big), \qquad R(z) = \frac{1 + z/2}{1 - z/2}.$$

It is A-stable and second order.

![The stability regions of four methods in the complex z-plane, where z = h times lambda. Euler: a disk of radius 1 centered at −1. RK4: a larger rounded region reaching to about −2.8 on the real axis. Backward Euler: everything outside a disk of radius 1 centered at +1, which includes the whole left half-plane. Trapezoidal: exactly the left half-plane.](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The shaded parts are where $\lvert R(z)\rvert \le 1$. The explicit methods have small, bounded
regions; the two implicit methods contain the entire left half-plane.

### Example 2

Apply backward Euler with $h = 0.1$ to $y' = -1000(y - \cos t)$, $y(0) = 0$.

The equation is linear in $y_{n+1}$, so solve for it:
$$y_{n+1} = y_n - 100\big(y_{n+1} - \cos t_{n+1}\big) \;\Longrightarrow\; y_{n+1} = \frac{y_n + 100\cos t_{n+1}}{101}.$$

- $y_1 = \dfrac{0 + 100\cos 0.1}{101} \approx 0.9852$ (exact $0.9951$)
- $y_2 = \dfrac{0.9852 + 100\cos 0.2}{101} \approx 0.9801$ (exact $0.9803$)
- $y_3 \approx 0.9556$ (exact $0.9556$)

The first step can't follow the transient, which lasts far less than one step, but after that
the numbers sit on the smooth solution, using a step 50 times larger than Euler's stability
limit.

```plot
{"x": [0, 1], "y": [0, 1.1], "xLabel": "t", "yLabel": "y", "functions": [{"f": "(1000000cos(x) + 1000sin(x))/1000001 - (1000000/1000001)exp(-1000x)"}], "labels": [{"at": [0.3, 0.72], "text": "exact solution"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 0]}, {"at": [0.1, 0.9852]}, {"at": [0.2, 0.9801]}, {"at": [0.3, 0.9556]}, {"at": [0.4, 0.9214]}, {"at": [0.5, 0.878]}, {"at": [0.6, 0.8259]}, {"at": [0.7, 0.7654]}, {"at": [0.8, 0.6974]}, {"at": [0.9, 0.6224]}, {"at": [1, 0.5411]}], "caption": "Backward Euler with h = 0.1 (dots) on y′ = −1000(y − cos t). The exact solution jumps almost instantly from 0 to near cos t; the dots follow it from the first step on. Euler with the same step would be near 970,000 by t = 0.3."}
```

### Example 3

Try the trapezoidal method on the same problem with $h = 0.1$. Here $z = -100$, so
$R(-100) = \dfrac{1 - 50}{1 + 50} = -\dfrac{49}{51} \approx -0.96$. The method is stable, but the
initial transient is damped by only 4% per step and flips sign each time. Computing:
$y_1 \approx 1.956$, $y_2 \approx 0.057$, $y_3 \approx 1.843$, while the true values are near
$0.99$, $0.98$, $0.96$. The error swings by about $\pm 0.9$ for many steps. Backward Euler's
$R(-100) = \tfrac1{101}$ wipes the transient out at once.

The difference is the limit as $z \to -\infty$: backward Euler's $R(z) \to 0$, but the
trapezoidal $R(z) \to -1$. A method that is A-stable and also has $R(z) \to 0$ as $\lvert z\rvert \to \infty$ is called
**[[L-stable]]**. Many widely used stiff solvers are built on backward-Euler-like formulas, such as
the **[[backward differentiation formulas]]** (BDF), which use several earlier points to reach higher
order.

## The price: solving an equation each step

When $f$ is linear in $y$, as above, the implicit equation is solved with algebra. When it is
nonlinear, each step needs a root-finder, usually Newton's method.

### Example 4

Take one backward Euler step with $h = 0.25$ for $y' = -2y^2$, $y(0) = 1$.

- The step equation is $Y = 1 + 0.25(-2Y^2) = 1 - 0.5Y^2$, so $0.5Y^2 + Y - 1 = 0$.
- Quadratic formula: $Y = -1 \pm \sqrt{3}$. Take the root near $y_0 = 1$:
  $Y = \sqrt3 - 1 \approx 0.7321$.
- Newton's method finds it without the formula: with $g(Y) = 0.5Y^2 + Y - 1$ and
  $g'(Y) = Y + 1$, start at $Y_0 = y_0 = 1$: $Y_1 = 1 - \tfrac{0.5}{2} = 0.75$, then
  $Y_2 = 0.75 - \tfrac{0.03125}{1.75} \approx 0.73214$, already within $10^{-4}$.
- The exact value is $y(0.25) = \tfrac{1}{1 + 2(0.25)} = \tfrac23 \approx 0.6667$; explicit Euler
  gives $1 - 0.5 = 0.5$.

So an implicit step costs more: a few evaluations of $f$ and of $\partial f/\partial y$, and a
linear solve for systems. On a stiff problem that is a bargain, because the steps can be
hundreds of times longer. On a non-stiff problem it is wasted effort, and an explicit method
such as RK4 is the better choice. Software libraries offer both kinds: SciPy's `solve_ivp`, for
example, has the explicit `RK45` as its default and the implicit `Radau` and `BDF` for stiff
problems.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: Is a problem stiff?
  accDescr: Estimate the step size that accuracy needs and the step size that an explicit method needs for stability, which is about 2 divided by the size of the most negative rate in the problem. If stability forces a much smaller step than accuracy, the problem is stiff and an implicit method such as backward Euler, the trapezoidal method or a BDF solver is the better choice. If not, use an explicit method such as RK4.
  A["Step size accuracy needs"] --> C{"Stability limit much smaller?"}
  B["Explicit stability limit, about 2/|λ|"] --> C
  C -- "yes: stiff" --> D["Implicit method: backward Euler, trapezoidal, BDF"]
  C -- "no" --> E["Explicit method such as RK4"]
```

## Common mistakes

- **Thinking implicit means more accurate.** Backward Euler has the same first order as Euler.
  Implicit methods win on stability, not accuracy per step.
- **Thinking stiff means fast-changing.** The solution you want is usually smooth. Stiffness is a
  fast component that has already died out but still limits explicit methods.
- **Taking the wrong root.** An implicit step can have several solutions; the right one is near
  $y_n$ (start Newton's method there).
- **Assuming A-stable is enough.** The trapezoidal method is A-stable but lets stiff transients
  ring for many steps.

## Key points

- On $y' = \lambda y$, a one-step method gives $y_{n+1} = R(z)y_n$ with $z = h\lambda$; it is stable
  where $\lvert R(z)\rvert \le 1$.
- Explicit methods have bounded regions: Euler and improved Euler need $h \le 2/\lvert\lambda\rvert$,
  RK4 about $2.785/\lvert\lambda\rvert$.
- A problem is stiff when stability, not accuracy, limits an explicit method's step.
- Backward Euler $R = 1/(1 - z)$ and trapezoidal $R = (1 + z/2)/(1 - z/2)$ are A-stable; backward
  Euler is also L-stable.
- Implicit steps require solving an equation (Newton's method when $f$ is nonlinear).

lessons.title: Error estimates and adaptive step size
lessons.body:
Lesson 16 mentioned a trick: compute with step $h$ and with step $h/2$, and the difference
between the answers shows roughly how large the error is. This lesson makes that precise, then
turns it into the way real solvers work. They estimate the error of every step as they go and
choose the next step size so the error stays near a target the user sets. Small steps where
the solution changes quickly, large steps where it is calm, and no need to know in advance
which is which.

## Richardson's error estimate

For a method of order $p$, the result at a fixed time $T$ behaves for small $h$ like

$$A(h) \approx y(T) + Ch^p,$$

where $C$ depends on the problem but hardly on $h$. Halving the step gives
$A(h/2) \approx y(T) + Ch^p/2^p$. Subtracting the two eliminates $y(T)$:

$$A(h) - A(h/2) \approx Ch^p\left(1 - \frac{1}{2^p}\right) = \frac{Ch^p}{2^p}(2^p - 1).$$

Since $Ch^p/2^p$ is the error of $A(h/2)$, we get an estimate of that error from the two
computed numbers alone:

$$y(T) - A(h/2) \approx \frac{A(h/2) - A(h)}{2^p - 1}.$$

Adding this estimate to $A(h/2)$ gives an improved value. That step is called
**[[Richardson extrapolation]]**, after the English scientist Lewis Fry Richardson, who used it in the early
twentieth century.

$$A_{\text{better}} = A(h/2) + \frac{A(h/2) - A(h)}{2^p - 1}.$$

### Example 1

For $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$, the true value is $y(1) = e \approx 2.718282$.

**Euler** ($p = 1$): $A(0.1) = 2.593742$ and $A(0.05) = 2.653298$ (Lesson 16).

- Estimated error of $A(0.05)$: $\dfrac{2.653298 - 2.593742}{2^1 - 1} = 0.059556$. The actual error
  is $0.064984$, so the estimate is right to within about 10%.
- Extrapolated: $2.653298 + 0.059556 = 2.712854$, error $0.0054$, about twelve times smaller
  than the error of $A(0.05)$.

**[[Improved Euler]]** ($p = 2$): $A(0.1) = 2.714081$ and $A(0.05) = 2.717191$.

- Estimated error of $A(0.05)$: $\dfrac{2.717191 - 2.714081}{2^2 - 1} = 0.001037$. Actual:
  $0.001091$.
- Extrapolated: $2.717191 + 0.001037 = 2.718228$, error about $5 \times 10^{-5}$.

The estimate is only as good as the assumption $A(h) \approx y(T) + Ch^p$, which needs $h$ small
enough. If the two answers disagree wildly, the estimate means little and the step should be
cut further.

## Embedded pairs: an error estimate for free

Step doubling triples the work. A cheaper idea is to run two methods of different orders that
share their slope evaluations. The simplest **[[embedded pair]]** is Heun–Euler. One improved Euler
step already computes $k_1 = f(t_n, y_n)$ and $k_2 = f(t_n + h,\ y_n + hk_1)$, so both

$$y_E = y_n + hk_1 \quad\text{(Euler, order 1)} \qquad\text{and}\qquad z = y_n + \frac h2(k_1 + k_2) \quad\text{(Heun, order 2)}$$

come at no extra cost. Because $z$ is much more accurate than $y_E$, the difference

$$\text{est} = \lvert z - y_E\rvert = \frac h2\,\lvert k_2 - k_1\rvert$$

is a good estimate of the local error of the Euler step. Professional codes use the same idea
with higher orders. The Runge–Kutta–Fehlberg method (RKF45) pairs orders 4 and 5. The
**[[Dormand–Prince method]]**, a 5(4) pair, is the engine of MATLAB's `ode45` and of SciPy's default
`RK45`. It has seven stages, but the last slope of one step is the first slope of the next, so
it costs about six evaluations of $f$ per step.

## Choosing the next step size

The error estimate belongs to the lower-order method, of order $p$, whose local error is about
$Ch^{p+1}$ (one power more than its global order; Lesson 16). Suppose a step of size $h$
produced the estimate est, and we want the local error to be at most a **[[tolerance]]** tol. The
step size that would have made $Ch_{\text{new}}^{p+1} = \text{tol}$ satisfies
$\left(h_{\text{new}}/h\right)^{p+1} = \text{tol}/\text{est}$, so

$$h_{\text{new}} = \sigma\, h\left(\frac{\text{tol}}{\text{est}}\right)^{1/(p+1)}.$$

The **[[safety factor]]** $\sigma$, typically 0.8 or 0.9, aims a little below the tolerance so
that fewer steps fail. Codes also cap how fast $h$ may grow or shrink in one go. The full loop
is **[[adaptive step-size control]]**:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: The adaptive step-size loop
  accDescr: From the current point, take a step of size h with both methods of the embedded pair and compute the error estimate. If the estimate is at most the tolerance, accept the step and move forward, usually keeping the higher-order value. If it is larger, reject the step and stay at the same point. In both cases compute a new step size from the formula h new equals safety factor times h times the tolerance over the estimate, to the power 1 over p plus 1, and repeat until the end of the interval.
  A["Current point, step size h"] --> B["Step with both methods of the pair"]
  B --> C["Estimate = difference of the two results"]
  C --> D{"Estimate at most tol?"}
  D -- "yes" --> E["Accept: move to the new point"]
  D -- "no" --> F["Reject: stay at the same point"]
  E --> G["New h = σ h (tol / est) to the power 1/(p + 1)"]
  F --> G
  G --> A
```

After an accepted step, codes usually continue from the higher-order value $z$ rather than the
lower-order one whose error was estimated. This is called **[[local extrapolation]]**: the error
estimate is then a little pessimistic, which errs on the safe side.

### Example 2

Solve $y' = t - y$, $y(0) = 1$ with the Heun–Euler pair ($p = 1$), tolerance $0.001$, safety
factor $0.9$, and a first try of $h = 0.2$.

First try, $h = 0.2$:

- $k_1 = 0 - 1 = -1$, so $y_E = 1 + 0.2(-1) = 0.8$.
- $k_2 = f(0.2,\ 0.8) = 0.2 - 0.8 = -0.6$, so $z = 1 + 0.1(-1 - 0.6) = 0.84$.
- est $= \lvert 0.84 - 0.8\rvert = 0.04 > 0.001$: **reject**.
- $h_{\text{new}} = 0.9(0.2)\left(\dfrac{0.001}{0.04}\right)^{1/2} = 0.18 \times 0.158 \approx 0.0285$.

Second try, $h = 0.0285$ (more precisely $0.02846$), from the same point:

- $y_E = 1 - 0.02846 = 0.97154$; $k_2 = 0.02846 - 0.97154 = -0.94308$.
- est $= \tfrac{0.02846}{2}\lvert -0.94308 - (-1)\rvert \approx 0.00081 \le 0.001$: **accept**, and
  continue from $z \approx 0.97235$ at $t \approx 0.0285$.
- The next step is $0.9(0.02846)(0.001/0.00081)^{1/2} \approx 0.0285$ again; as the solution
  levels off, the steps slowly lengthen.

The exact solution $y = t - 1 + 2e^{-t}$ gives $y(0.2) \approx 0.8375$, so the rejected Euler value
$0.8$ really was off by about $0.04$, just as estimated.

### Example 3

The logistic equation $y' = 10y(1 - y)$, $y(0) = 0.01$ rises steeply around $t = 0.46$ and is
nearly flat before and after. Running the same Heun–Euler controller from $t = 0$ to $2$ with
tolerance $0.005$ takes 31 accepted steps (plus 8 rejected tries). The steps shrink to about
$0.03$ on the steep part and grow to about $0.23$ near the end.

```plot
{"x": [0, 2], "y": [0, 1.1], "xLabel": "t", "yLabel": "y", "functions": [{"f": "1/(1 + 99exp(-10x))"}], "labels": [{"at": [1.4, 0.8], "text": "exact solution"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 0.01]}, {"at": [0.1, 0.025]}, {"at": [0.16, 0.043]}, {"at": [0.207, 0.067]}, {"at": [0.246, 0.095]}, {"at": [0.281, 0.13]}, {"at": [0.316, 0.173]}, {"at": [0.348, 0.224]}, {"at": [0.378, 0.281]}, {"at": [0.409, 0.346]}, {"at": [0.442, 0.423]}, {"at": [0.481, 0.519]}, {"at": [0.519, 0.612]}, {"at": [0.55, 0.683]}, {"at": [0.58, 0.742]}, {"at": [0.609, 0.794]}, {"at": [0.637, 0.836]}, {"at": [0.665, 0.87]}, {"at": [0.694, 0.899]}, {"at": [0.724, 0.923]}, {"at": [0.757, 0.943]}, {"at": [0.794, 0.96]}, {"at": [0.834, 0.972]}, {"at": [0.882, 0.982]}, {"at": [0.938, 0.989]}, {"at": [1.007, 0.994]}, {"at": [1.095, 0.997]}, {"at": [1.214, 0.998]}, {"at": [1.379, 0.999]}, {"at": [1.609, 0.999]}, {"at": [1.844, 0.998]}, {"at": [2, 0.999]}], "caption": "Adaptive Heun–Euler steps (dots) on y′ = 10y(1 − y) with tolerance 0.005: crowded where the curve is steep, spread out where it is flat."}
```

Two honest remarks. First, the largest error along the way is about $0.034$, several times the
tolerance; see the next section. Second, on a mild problem like this one a well-chosen fixed
step does about as well. Adaptivity pays off when the quiet and busy stretches are very
different in length, or when you don't know in advance where the busy parts are.

## What the tolerance does and doesn't control

- **It limits local error, not global error.** Each step's error is kept near tol, but errors
  from all steps accumulate (Lesson 16), and an unstable solution can amplify them. A standard
  check is to solve again with a tolerance ten times smaller; the digits that don't change can be
  trusted. This is Richardson's idea applied to the whole run.
- **It is usually mixed.** Software accepts a step when the error is below
  $\text{atol} + \text{rtol}\cdot\lvert y\rvert$: an absolute part for values near zero and a relative
  part for large values. SciPy's `solve_ivp`, for example, defaults to $\text{rtol} = 10^{-3}$ and
  $\text{atol} = 10^{-6}$.
- **It cannot cure stiffness.** On a stiff problem an explicit adaptive solver shrinks $h$ down
  to the stability limit and keeps it there, taking huge numbers of tiny steps (often with many
  rejections) while the solution looks smooth. That pattern is a sign to switch to an implicit
  method (the previous honors lesson).

## Common mistakes

- **Wrong exponent.** The step formula uses $1/(p + 1)$, where $p$ is the order of the method
  whose error is estimated, because local error is one power higher than the global order.
- **Wrong denominator.** Richardson's estimate divides by $2^p - 1$, not $2^p$.
- **Advancing after a failed step.** A rejected step is retried from the *same* point with a
  smaller $h$.
- **Reading the tolerance as a guarantee.** The final answer can be off by more than tol.

## Key points

- Richardson: for order $p$, $y(T) - A(h/2) \approx \dfrac{A(h/2) - A(h)}{2^p - 1}$; adding it gives
  a better value.
- Embedded pairs (Heun–Euler, RKF45, Dormand–Prince) get an error estimate from shared slopes.
- Heun–Euler estimate: $\tfrac h2\lvert k_2 - k_1\rvert$.
- New step: $h_{\text{new}} = \sigma h\,(\text{tol}/\text{est})^{1/(p+1)}$; reject and retry if
  est $>$ tol.
- Tolerances control local error; check global accuracy by tightening the tolerance.

lessons.title: Second-order linear equations and the Wronskian
lessons.body:
## Why second order?

Newton's second law, $F = ma$, sets an *acceleration*, a second derivative. So the
motion of anything driven by forces, from a car suspension to a guitar string to the
current in a radio's tuning circuit, is governed by second-order equations. This module
develops the theory and methods for the **[[second-order linear equation]]**

$$y'' + p(t)y' + q(t)y = g(t).$$

This lesson is about structure: what the set of solutions looks like and how to know when
you've found all of them. The next three lessons find solutions explicitly when the
coefficients are constants.

## Existence and uniqueness

**Theorem.** If $p$, $q$ and $g$ are continuous on an open interval $I$ containing $t_0$,
then the IVP

$$y'' + py' + qy = g, \qquad y(t_0) = y_0, \quad y'(t_0) = y_0'$$

has exactly one solution, and it exists on all of $I$.

Two initial conditions, position and velocity, are needed: that's the second-order
version of Lesson 7's theorem. As before, linearity guarantees the solution lasts across
the whole interval.

## The homogeneous equation and superposition

Write $L[y] = y'' + py' + qy$. Then $L$ is a **[[linear operator]]**: for constants $c_1, c_2$,

$$L[c_1y_1 + c_2y_2] = c_1L[y_1] + c_2L[y_2],$$

because differentiation respects sums and constant multiples. So if $y_1$ and $y_2$ solve
the homogeneous equation $L[y] = 0$, then so does every **[[linear combination]]**
$c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$. This is the **[[principle of superposition]]**.

## When do two solutions give all solutions?

Given two solutions $y_1$, $y_2$ of $L[y] = 0$, can we fit *any* initial conditions with
$c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$? We need $c_1, c_2$ with

$$c_1y_1(t_0) + c_2y_2(t_0) = y_0, \qquad c_1y_1'(t_0) + c_2y_2'(t_0) = y_0'.$$

This $2 \times 2$ linear system has a unique solution for every right side exactly when
its determinant is nonzero. That determinant is the **[[Wronskian]]**:

$$W(y_1, y_2)(t) = \begin{vmatrix} y_1 & y_2 \\ y_1' & y_2' \end{vmatrix} = y_1y_2' - y_1'y_2.$$

**Theorem.** If $y_1$, $y_2$ solve $L[y] = 0$ on $I$ and $W(y_1, y_2)(t_0) \ne 0$ for some
$t_0$ in $I$, then every solution on $I$ has the form $y = c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$.

Such a pair is a **[[fundamental set of solutions]]**, and $c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$ is the
**[[general solution]]**. The proof: take any solution $\phi$; choose $c_1, c_2$ to match
$\phi(t_0)$ and $\phi'(t_0)$ (possible because $W \ne 0$); then $\phi$ and
$c_1y_1 + c_2y_2$ solve the same IVP, so by uniqueness they're equal.

### Abel's theorem

For solutions of $L[y] = 0$, the Wronskian satisfies $W' = -p(t)W$ (a short computation),
so

$$W(t) = Ce^{-\int p(t)\,dt}.$$

An exponential is never zero, so $W$ is either zero everywhere on $I$ or never zero.
That's why it's enough to check one point.

## Linear independence

Two functions are **[[linearly dependent]]** if one is a constant multiple of the other, and
**[[linearly independent]]** otherwise. For solutions of $L[y] = 0$, being a fundamental set
is the same as being linearly independent. If $y_2 = ky_1$, then
$W = y_1(ky_1') - y_1'(ky_1) = 0$.

### Example 1

Show that $y_1 = e^{2t}$ and $y_2 = e^{-3t}$ form a fundamental set for
$y'' + y' - 6y = 0$, and solve the IVP $y(0) = 1$, $y'(0) = 7$.

- Check they're solutions: for $e^{2t}$, $4 + 2 - 6 = 0$; for $e^{-3t}$, $9 - 3 - 6 = 0$. ✓
- Wronskian: $W = e^{2t}(-3e^{-3t}) - (2e^{2t})e^{-3t} = -5e^{-t} \ne 0$. Fundamental set.
- General solution $y = c_1e^{2t} + c_2e^{-3t}$, with $y' = 2c_1e^{2t} - 3c_2e^{-3t}$.
- Conditions: $c_1 + c_2 = 1$, $2c_1 - 3c_2 = 7$. Adding 3 times the first: $5c_1 = 10$, so
  $c_1 = 2$, $c_2 = -1$.
- Answer: $y = 2e^{2t} - e^{-3t}$.

Abel's theorem check: $p = 1$, so $W = Ce^{-t}$, matching $-5e^{-t}$.

The figure shows superposition at work: the solution is the sum of the two pieces
$2e^{2t}$ and $-e^{-3t}$, and it passes through $(0, 1)$ as required.

```plot
{"x": [-1, 1], "y": [-20, 15], "xLabel": "t", "functions": [{"f": "2exp(2x)", "dashed": true}, {"f": "-exp(-3x)", "dashed": true}, {"f": "2exp(2x) - exp(-3x)", "label": "y = 2e^(2t) − e^(−3t)"}], "points": [{"at": [0, 1]}], "labels": [{"at": [-0.3, 5], "text": "(0, 1)"}], "caption": "The IVP solution (solid) is the sum of 2e^(2t) (dashed, rising) and −e^(−3t) (dashed, below the axis)."}
```

### Example 2

Are $y_1 = \cos 3t$ and $y_2 = \sin 3t$ a fundamental set for $y'' + 9y = 0$?

- Both solve it ($y'' = -9y$ for each).
- $W = \cos 3t \cdot 3\cos 3t - (-3\sin 3t)\sin 3t = 3(\cos^2 3t + \sin^2 3t) = 3$. Never zero.
- Yes. General solution $y = c_1\cos 3t + c_2\sin 3t$.

### Example 3

$y_1 = t$ and $y_2 = t^2$ have $W = t \cdot 2t - 1 \cdot t^2 = t^2$, which is zero at
$t = 0$ but not elsewhere. Abel's theorem says that's impossible for two solutions of an
equation $y'' + py' + qy = 0$ with $p, q$ continuous on an interval containing 0. Indeed
they solve $t^2y'' - 2ty' + 2y = 0$, whose standard form has $p = -2/t$, discontinuous at
0. On $(0, \infty)$ they form a fundamental set.

## The nonhomogeneous equation

If $Y_1$ and $Y_2$ both solve $L[y] = g$, then $L[Y_1 - Y_2] = g - g = 0$: their difference
solves the homogeneous equation. So every solution of $L[y] = g$ has the form

$$y = \underbrace{c_1y_1 + c_2y_2}_{y_c,\ \text{complementary solution}} + \underbrace{Y(t)}_{\text{particular solution}}.$$

The homogeneous part is called the **[[complementary solution]]** $y_c$; $Y$ is any one
**[[particular solution]]**. You met this structure for first-order equations in Lesson 8.
Module 6 finds particular solutions; Lessons 19–21 find $y_c$.

The flowchart puts the whole procedure of this lesson in one place.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  accTitle: From two solutions to the solution of an initial value problem
  accDescr: Start with two solutions y1 and y2 of the homogeneous equation. Compute their Wronskian at one point. If it is zero, they are not a fundamental set, so find a different second solution and test again. If it is nonzero, the general solution of the homogeneous equation is c1 y1 + c2 y2. If the equation has a forcing term g, add one particular solution Y. Finally fit c1 and c2 to the two initial conditions.
  A["Two solutions y1, y2 of L[y] = 0"] --> B["Compute W = y1 y2' - y1' y2 at one point"]
  B --> C{"Is W zero?"}
  C -- "yes" --> D["Not a fundamental set: find another solution"]
  D --> B
  C -- "no" --> E["Fundamental set: y_c = c1 y1 + c2 y2"]
  E --> F{"Is g zero?"}
  F -- "yes" --> H["y = y_c"]
  F -- "no" --> G["y = y_c + Y, one particular solution Y"]
  H --> I["Fit c1, c2 to y(t0) and y'(t0)"]
  G --> I
```

## Common mistakes

- **Applying superposition to nonhomogeneous equations.** The sum of two solutions of
  $L[y] = g$ solves $L[y] = 2g$, not $L[y] = g$.
- **Wronskian sign or order.** $W = y_1y_2' - y_1'y_2$; swapping $y_1$ and $y_2$ flips the
  sign, which doesn't affect whether it's zero.
